title: The Parity Check
primary_metric: extra overhead bits transmitted per additional error pattern caught

options.A: The Featherweight Check — a single even-parity bit appended to every byte of sensor data
options.B: The Full-Frame Guard — a 4-byte CRC-32 frame check sequence appended once per packet, the same scheme IEEE 802.11 uses

sources.claim: IEEE 802.11 MAC frame FCS field length
sources.title: IEEE 802.11 Mac Frame
sources.note: Tutorial/reference site, not the IEEE standard document itself; corroborated independently by S2 (Wikipedia's CRC page, which separately confirms ISO/IEC/IEEE 802-11 uses CRC-32). States the FCS is a 4-byte, 32-bit CRC calculated over the MAC header and frame body.

sources.claim: CRC-32 generator polynomial and its use by IEEE 802.11/802.3
sources.title: Cyclic redundancy check
sources.note: Article's CRC-32 parametrization table explicitly lists ISO/IEC/IEEE 802-11 (Wi-Fi) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 802-3 (Ethernet) among the standards using this exact polynomial.

sources.value: 8 data bits + 1 parity bit (1 bit per 8 data bits = 12.5% overhead)
sources.title: Parity bit
sources.note: Article states '8 bits of data plus a parity bit can convey all 8-bit byte values' and describes UART/serial hardware generating/checking parity this way. The 12.5% figure is the case's own arithmetic (1 bit / 8 data bits), not itself independently published.

sources.claim: Receiver-sensitivity-defining packet error rate for a small wireless sensor-network standard, used to derive a representative per-bit error rate
sources.value: 1% PER at 20-byte (160-bit) reference packet => derived per-bit BER ~6.3e-5
sources.org: ns-3 Network Simulator project (secondary source confirming IEEE Std 802.15.4-2006 §6.1.7/E.4.1.7)

sources.note: IEEE 802.15.4 (LR-WPAN) is a different real standard than this case's fictional satellite-IoT link — applied by analogy as the best available real anchor for 'a small LPWAN/sensor-network class link', not a direct measurement of this case's own device. Per-bit BER derived from 1-(1-0.01)^(1/160) ~= 6.28e-5, rounded to 6e-5 for Appendix E's stated value. Web search also surfaced real published figures for general wireless links spanning roughly 1e-6 (well-provisioned) to 1e-3 (marginal, about to be dropped) and a commonly cited 'typical wireless link' figure of ~1e-5 — used to bound Appendix E's disclosed plausible range.

reinforcement_note: The originating concept sheet (CONCEPTS_network-science_2026-09-12b.md, C1) identified number-sense-even, number-sense-odd, and number-sense-numbers-and-counting-digit as the group's remaining thin skills, each at n=1 (each covered by exactly one prior case — number-sense-numbers-and-counting-digit by 'Key Length'). Per SPEC §4, new_coverage[] is strictly the n==0 subset; since these are n=1 (already covered once), none qualify under the strict test, so new_coverage[] is correctly empty here. This case ships as a REINFORCEMENT case — a second real data point on each of the group's thin skills, taking them from n=1 to n=2 — following the identical, already-established project resolution documented in cases/pixel-snap/LEARNING_GOALS.md and cases/the-repeat-match/case.json for the same situation. deliverables.text: A byte-level worked table: for a set of sample sensor data bytes (Appendix B), the number of 1-bits in each byte, whether that count is EVEN or ODD, and the single parity bit the Featherweight Check would append.

A 'silent miss' demonstration: at least one worked example, built from Appendix B's sample bytes, of a corrupted byte where an EVEN number of bits flipped, showing the error the Featherweight Check misses but the Full-Frame Guard catches.

An overhead-vs-packet-size comparison table across the packet sizes in Appendix C: total data bits, Featherweight Check overhead bits, Full-Frame Guard overhead bits, and overhead as a percent of the transmitted frame, for each scheme at each size.
A bits-to-decimal-digits comparison: the maximum number of decimal digits needed to write out the largest possible check value for each scheme (a single parity bit vs. a 32-bit CRC value).

A break-even packet-size calculation and recommendation: using Appendix E's stated per-bit error rate to estimate the probability a byte suffers an even number of bit flips, compute overhead bits per additional error pattern caught for each scheme, and identify the packet size where the two schemes cross.

balance.argument_a: The Featherweight Check's overhead is fixed and tiny per byte (a small, near-constant percentage of the data stream — Appendix A). On Renata's smallest packets, its total added bits are far fewer than the Full-Frame Guard's flat 4-byte (32-bit) tax, which does not shrink with packet size. If the per-bit error rate is low enough, the probability of an even (undetected) number of flips per byte may be small enough that the cheap scheme's blind spot rarely costs anything in practice.
balance.argument_b: The Full-Frame Guard catches essentially all realistic error patterns, including the entire class of even-bit-flip errors the Featherweight Check is structurally blind to — not a rare edge case, but a gap that exists by construction on every single byte. Its fixed 32-bit cost is trivial as a fraction of a large packet: at Appendix C's 125-byte and 222-byte packet sizes, that same flat 32-bit tax is a far smaller share of the total transmission than it is at 35 bytes, so several of Renata's real packet sizes make the fixed cost cheaper per byte than the Featherweight Check's per-byte overhead, not more expensive.
balance.margin_basis: For each scheme, compute P(scheme catches the frame's corruption) / (overhead bits that scheme adds) — this case's own 'catches more corrupted frames per bit spent' framing (Background). Featherweight Check misses a frame only if every corrupted byte happens to have an EVEN, nonzero flip count (peven(p) = 0.5*(1+(1-2p)^8) per byte, per Appendix E's stated rate); Full-Frame Guard catches essentially all realistic corruption regardless of pattern (Appendix A). Compare the two per-bit efficiencies directly at each Appendix C packet size. The schemes' exact arithmetic tie point (1 bit/byte x n bytes = 32 bits) is n=32 bytes — an earlier draft set Appendix C row 2 exactly there and reported a razor-thin 0.02% margin, a coin-flip result that risked a fresh solver landing on either side; MA2 was retuned to n=35 bytes, close enough to stay a live, non-landslide comparison but far enough from the tie point to land inside SPEC section 2's ~5-15% target band. margin_pct is reported at this size (35 bytes).
balance.winner_at_reported_size: B (Full-Frame Guard) — margin 9.40% at Appendix E's stated 6e-5 error rate; ranges 9.38%-9.71% across the full disclosed 1e-6-1e-3 range, per sensitivity_model.py's Probe 5 sweep — never flips to A within that range, and stays comfortably inside SPEC section 2's ~5-15% target band and well under its 20% cap throughout
balance.winner_by_packet_size: A (Featherweight Check) wins outright at n=11 bytes (margin ~191%, stable across the full error-rate range); B (Full-Frame Guard) wins outright at n=125 and n=222 bytes (margins ~291% and ~594% respectively, both stable across the full error-rate range) — packet size, not the error-rate assumption, is what determines the winner away from the n=32 tie point (with n=35, the case's reported size, being the winner-B side closest to that tie point that still lands the margin in SPEC section 2's target band).
balance.robustness_check: PASSED. Per FACILITATOR.md's mandatory Robustness Check (added after cases/the-overlap-call was killed for an assumption-fragile margin), sensitivity_model.py sweeps Appendix E's per-bit error rate (MA1) across its full disclosed real-world-plausible range (1e-6 to 1e-3, spanning three orders of magnitude) at the reported packet size (35 bytes, MA2). The winner (B) does not flip anywhere in that range; margin stays between 9.38% and 9.71% throughout, moving by less than 0.4 percentage points across three orders of magnitude of error-rate assumption. This case is NOT in the-overlap-call's fragility class — see RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full sweep table and cases/the-parity-check/sensitivity_model.py for the runnable model.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Representative per-bit error rate for this class of link (Appendix E)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public per-bit BER figure exists for this fictional link. Derived from IEEE Std 802.15.4-2006's own receiver-sensitivity definition (1% PER at a 20-byte/160-bit reference packet, S6) — a real standard for a comparable class of low-power wireless sensor network, applied here by analogy: per-bit BER = 1-(1-0.01)^(1/160) ~= 6.28e-5, rounded to 6e-5. Real published BER figures for wireless/LPWAN links found during research range from ~1e-6 (well-provisioned) to ~1e-3 (marginal/about-to-drop), with ~1e-5 commonly cited as 'typical' — this range bounds the disclosed plausible interval.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value at some packet sizes and not others. sensitivity_model.py's Probe 5 sweep (RESEARCH_LOG.md) confirms the winner at the case's reported packet size (35 bytes, MA2) does NOT flip anywhere across the full disclosed range (1e-6 to 1e-3) — margin stays between 9.38% and 9.71%, always favoring the Full-Frame Guard.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Second candidate packet size (Appendix C, row 2)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single public 'typical mid-size payload' figure is specific to this fictional uplink. Chosen within the real payload envelope this class of device supports (Appendix C rows 1 and 4, sourced to S4/S5), comparable to a compact multi-field reading (e.g. temperature + humidity + battery voltage + a short device/sequence ID). An earlier draft set this value to the schemes' exact arithmetic tie point (32 bytes: 1 bit/byte x 32 bytes = the CRC's 32-bit overhead), which produced a razor-thin 0.02% margin — a coin-flip result. Retuned to 35 bytes, close enough to the tie point to remain a genuinely live comparison (not a landslide, unlike n=11/125/222) but far enough off it to land inside SPEC section 2's ~5-15% target balance band (9.40% at the stated error rate).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value — recompute D3/D5 with a somewhat larger and somewhat smaller packet size and compare which option wins. Confirmed stable across the full disclosed error-rate range at n=35 (margin 9.38%-9.71%, per sensitivity_model.py).

sensitivity_note: ROBUSTNESS CHECK COMPLETE (2026-09-13, retuned same day) — case-research first landed Appendix C row 2 exactly at the schemes' geometric tie point (32 bytes), which produced a razor-thin 0.02% margin — a coin-flip result flagged as too fragile for a fresh solver to land on reliably, the same failure shape as cases/the-overlap-call. MA2 was retuned to 35 bytes (see RESEARCH_LOG.md 'Retune' entry). sensitivity_model.py sweeps Appendix E's per-bit error rate (MA1) across its full disclosed real-world-plausible range (1e-6 to 1e-3, three orders of magnitude) at the case's reported packet size (35 bytes, Appendix C row 2 / MA2). RESULT: STABLE. The winner (B, Full-Frame Guard) never flips across that range; margin ranges 9.38%-9.71%, always favoring B — comfortably inside SPEC section 2's ~5-15% target band and well under its 20% cap throughout. The break-even packet size itself (where the two schemes' raw arithmetic exactly ties, 31.90-32.00 bytes across the swept range) is unchanged and unaffected by this retune — only which real/plausible size the case reports its margin at has moved. This case does NOT share cases/the-overlap-call's fragility (a margin that looked close but flipped under small, realistic assumption changes) — see RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full sweep table and case.json.balance.robustness_check for the summary. sensitivity_disclosure[] is correctly empty: no swept parameter flips the winner or breaches the SPEC §2 20% cap within its disclosed plausible range at the reported size.
